newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Sierra Leone talks collapse, junta defiant.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone talks collapse, junta defiant.

text.p: Envoys from Sierra Leone's West African neighbours broke off talks with its military rulers on Thursday and recommended tightening economic sanctions to force them to reinstate civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

Nigeria's foreign minister, Tom Ikimi, announced the collapse of the talks in Ivory Coast after military ruler Johnny Paul Koroma spoke of a transition of more than four years before a return to civilian rule in the former British colony.

"The committee (of four West African foreign ministers) expressed dismay at the announcement by the illegal regime in Freetown, while the meeting was still in session, of its decision to suspend the constitution of Sierra Leone and remain in office illegally until the year 2001," Ikimi said.
"It is an affront to ECOWAS (the Economic Community of West African States), it is an affront to Africa, it is an affront to the international community," he told reporters later.

The committee statement accused the junta of reneging on an agreement reached during a first round of talks on reinstating Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule.

"The committee found the new position of the Sierra Leonean delegation on the issue of the reinstatement of President Kabbah totally unacceptable," Ikimi said, reading the statement. He said the junta's envoys had no real maandate to negotiate.

The talks, the second round between the two sides to try to head off a showdown over the May 25 coup, began on Tuesday and ended abruptly after Koroma's defiant announcement in Sierra Leone's capital Freetown.

Ikimi said he and his follow foreign ministers from Ivory Coast, Ghana and Guinea would recommend to Nigeria's military ruler, Sani Abacha, the ECOWAS chairman, that an economic embargo should be tightened to ensure Kabbah's early return to power.

Koroma, in a statement from his ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council on state radio and television, said parliamentary elections would be held in February 2001, elections for a state council by May that year with presidential elections by November. He did not spell out the role of the state council.
Koroma said a ban on political parties would be lifted at least a couple of months before the parliamentary poll and the constitution would remain suspended until then.

"The AFRC will not be stampeded into hurrying matters beyond their appointed course," he said, adding that the junta was prepared to hand over to what he called "a properly ordered constitutional order."
"The AFRC stands ready to defend the sovereignty of Sierra Leone to the last drop of its blood," he said.
Sierra Leone's neighbours, led by regional giant Nigeria, have opted for dialogue and economic sanctions to press for Kabbah's reinstatement but they have not ruled out the military option.
Rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup which has been widely denounced abroad.

Nigerian-led troops are in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact. Their attempt to dislodge the coup leaders with a June 2 naval bombardment backfired when Sierra Leone soldiers and rebels attacked exposed Nigerian positions.
Since then, Nigeria has played the diplomatic card while sending extra troops to Sierra Leone. Korama called for the force to leave the country.
